operative_excerpt: imited amount of general farming work as required. [27] The JFCT did ultimately interview ADO in relation to the stock manager position. However, ADO was not appointed to that role. 3 Another Member of the Authority reviewed the relevant document and decided that the document was not in fact without prejudice correspondence. [28] Mr MacGillivray says that his professional opinion, having been involved in the interview process for the stock manager role, is that ADO is “wholly unsuited for the stock manager role…”. He refers to the introduction of a modern farming structure including the need for experience in modern technology feed budgeting, feed allocation and animal welfare. He says that ADO fell short in those areas, and referred to an assessment report produced in relation to the recruitment and interview process. [29] Mr Angland was also involved in the interview process for the stock manager role. He says he agrees with the content of Mr MacGillivray’s report, and that ADO was lacking in the skills for the stock manager position. He says he could not work with ADO in the stock manager position. Mr Angland also says that the role of general manager is very challenging and that he is not surprised ADO was not considered for that role. [30] ADO’s substantive claims are to be investigated at a future date and this determination deals only with their application for interim relief until such time as the substantive matter has been determined. ADO has provided an undertaking that they will abide by any order that the Authority may make in respect of damages.4 The approach to interim reinstatement [31] The Authority may order interim reinstatement pending the hearing of a personal grievance.5 In determining whether to make an order for interim reinstatement, the Authority must apply the law relating to interim injunctions having regard to the objects of the Act.6 [32] To determine this matter, I must consider whether there is a serious question to be tried7. That requires consideration as to whether ADO has an arguable case, firstly, as to the substantive application for unjustified dismissal, and if so, secondly, as to ADO’s application for permanent reinstatement.8 If ADO has a serious case to be tried, I must then exercise my discretion by considering where the balance of convenience 4 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 127(2) and (3); Suzanne May Buxton - undertaking in relation to application for interim reinstatement dated 15 September 2023, at [3]. 5 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 127(1). 6 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 127(4). 7 NZ Tax Refunds v Brooks Homes Limited [2013] NZCA 90, at [12] and [13]. 8 Western Bay of Plenty District Council v McInnes [2016] NZEmpC 36, at [8]. lies and, standing back from the case, consider what the overall justice of the case requires I do.9 Is there a serious case to be tried that ADO was unjustifiably dismissed? [33] ADO’s primary contentions as to the unjustified dismissal claim can be summarised as follows: (a) The restructuring process was used improperly to bring about ADO’s dismissal and was motivated by alleged misconduct and performance concerns; (b) The JFCT failed to consider suitable redeployment opportunities and the outcome was predetermined; (c) The disestablishment of ADO’s role was conflated with a failure to consider redeployment opportunities, rather than feedback as to the initial proposal being considered first; and (d) The process followed by the JFCT was neither fair nor reasonable, including because ADO was not provided information supporting the proposed restructure and therefore was not given an opportunity to provide meaningful feedback. [34] There is currently limited information as to an alleged disagreement on 2 October 2023 that is claimed to have preceded the announcement of the restructuring proposal on 4 October 2023. However, both the letter of 30 November 2023 sent by Mr Abraham, and the email sent by Mr Barham on 15 December 2023, are of some significance to the claim that the redundancy was not genuine and detail various complaints or comments as to alleged conduct and performance issues relating to ADO. [35] Mr Barham referred to his correspondence on 15 December 2023 in his affidavit in explaining the context in which that occurred. That correspondence must be treated with some caution at this juncture and the contents and associated evidence will no doubt be subject to scrutiny during any substantive investigation. However, it is the case that, on the material currently before the Authority, allegations relating to conduct and performance were also raised by Mr Abraham at an earlier stage. Based on the content of that correspondence, there is an arguable case that the dismissal was 9 Klissers Farmhouse Bakeries Ltd v Harvest Bakeries Ltd [1985] 2 NZLR 129 (CA); X v Y Ltd and the New Zealand Stock Exchange [1992] 1 ERNZ 862 (EmpC), at 872. substantively unjustified as having been motivated by, in significant part, matters other than genuine commercial considerations. [36] ADO submitted that the role and work they were performing remains unknown to the JFCT and that a fair and reasonable employer could not have disestablished ADO’s role where its understanding of that role was incorrect, including by reference to an email of 12 November 2023 that referred to ADO’s role as “farm general”. The letter attached to that email referred to “your role” without it being defined, as did the letter of 4 October 2023. [37] It is arguable that ADO was in fact performing the duties that are to be performed by the stock manager, and that ADO should either have continued in that role or should have been redeployed to the role of stock manager. It is arguable that the dismissal was unjustified on that basis. Further, it is strongly arguable that the JFCT did not genuinely consider redeployment having regard to the correspondence of 4 October 2023. [38] ADO has an arguable case that they should have been redeployed or appointed to the role of stock manager. However, having regard to the affidavit material in support of the JFCT’s opposition, I do not consider that aspect of his claim is more than moderately arguable. [39] ADO’s contention that the JFCT conflated the restructure with redeployment, and that it dismissed ADO prior to considering all options short of dismissal, is arguable. The letter of 4 October 2023 on one view confirmed that the possibility of other vacancies had already been considered, despite the same letter apparently being the first notification to ADO that a restructuring was being contemplated. ADO says that they were advised at the meeting on 10 November 2023 that their role was to be disestablished and that that occurred absent any consideration of redeployment. [40] ADO’s contention that Mr Barham did not have the required delegation from the JFCT Board is arguable. While I consider the position arguable, I consider it only weakly so given the evidence currently before the Authority. [41] It is also arguable that the JFCT failed to meaningfully consult with ADO as to the proposed restructuring. ADO submitted that plans to complete a modernisation process to be completed by March 2023 were publicly announced and that staff, including ADO, were not made aware of that in breach of good faith. It is arguable that Mr McDonald’s departure was foreseeable and that a fair and reasonable employer was obligated to engage with ADO before that happened. [42] Having considered the affidavit evidence and documents provided, I also consider that ADO has an arguable case that the dismissal was procedurally unjustified. ADO takes issue with an alleged failure to provide relevant information as part of the consultation process. The letter of 4 October 2023 contains what appears to be a very general overview of the purported basis for the restructuring. However, on the material currently before the Authority, it is arguable that information necessary for the purposes of genuine consultation was not provided to ADO and that ADO was not in a position to meaningfully consider and respond to the proposal. [43] While aspects of ADO’s claims differ in strength, I consider that overall, ADO has a strongly arguable case that they were unjustifiably dismissed. Does ADO have an arguable case for permanent reinstatement? [44] Section 125 of the Act requires the Authority to provide for reinstatement wherever practicable and reasonable.10 Reinstatement is the primary remedy. [45] ADO has a strongly arguable case that they were unjustifiably dismissed, including in relation to ADO’s claim that the dismissal was substantively unjustified. If successful with that claim I consider that ADO has a seriously arguable case as to permanent reinstatement. [46] At present, the stock manager position remains vacant. There is conflicting evidence as to ADO’s suitability to perform that role which will be subject to scrutiny later. The JFCT’s position is that ADO could not perform the role and ADO maintains that they are able to perform that, or another suitable role. [47] While the material currently before the Authority refers to alleged conduct and performance concerns, they have not been meaningfully advanced in the affidavit material. I do not consider those issues of significance in terms of the current assessment. 10 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 125. [48] ADO has a moderately arguable case for permanent reinstatement if successful in relation to claim that the dismissal lacked substantive justification. Such as ADO claims that the dismissal was procedurally unjustified, ADO has a weakly arguable case for permanent reinstatement. Who does the balance of convenience favour? [49] ADO says that they will lose income and be forced to vacate the farm accommodation. ADO also contends that they would be put into financial hardship, their funds would runout, and they would not have a home. ADO alluded to the difficulty they would have finding alternative employment, and in particular employment that comes with accommodation. [50] ADO maintains that they were willing to constructively engage in good faith if reinstated. They contend that being out of the workplace for any length of time would make it harder to reintegrate, including with a new manager. ADO also refers to the restoration of their professional reputation having been severely damaged, concern as to the costs of renting without an income, and the need to support their family and to meet other financial obligations. [51] Mr Barham says that the IEA required ADO to vacate the farmhouse upon termination of employment, but that the JFCT allowed him to stay until the completion of mediation. He says that the stock manager position is yet to be filled and that the two candidates for the role have indicated that to accept the role they would need to have the farmhouse made available for them to live in. He contends that the JFCT is unable to finalise its decision on vacant role until the farmhouse is vacated and that delay may result in waning interest in the role and a potential need for the recruitment process to restart. The evidence in the affidavit material falls short of reflecting that the candidates for the role are adamant as to the use of the farmhouse or that they have refused to accept the role on that basis. [52] Mr Barham says that ADO and their partner own a home in Wairoa and that he has seen three vehicles at the farms he believes are owned by them and referred to 74 properties being available for rent within 15km of the farm on TradeMe. He also says that ADO only worked 32 hours per week in their employed role, and that they performed other contract work including for the JFCT. He suggests that ADO would have no difficulty in obtaining other work, particularly given the impacts of Cyclone Gabrielle in the region. Mr Barham also referred to an incident in later January 2024 where 4 cattle were observed in the paddock adjacent to the farmhouse in breach of statutory TB regulations. [53] Mr Angland says managing Chesterhope without a stock manager is challenging and that he has been undertaking additional duties at Chesterhope. He says undertaking those additional duties himself over a significant period is not sustainable, despite currently being assisted by casual shepherds with dogs. He contends that the appointment of a stock manager is needed within the next month in order to make good progress with the modernisation plan. [54] While the JFCT assert a desire to restructure its operations and modernise its practices, I am not satisfied that its operations will be significantly impacted by ADO’s interim reinstatement. Regardless, accepting for present purposes the JFCT’s position that it will be unable to appoint a stock manager and that ADO is unable to fully perform that role, I am not persuaded that the impacts and inconvenience to the JFCT are matters that cannot be adequately dealt with in the context of damages. [55] Having regard to the issues identified by the JFCT in support of its opposition, I am not persuaded that, in balancing those with the ongoing and potentially significant impacts of ADO being out of the workplace for a significant period of time, that the JFCT’s concerns should be given any greater weight than those of ADO. [56] It may be that ADO is able, if not reinstated on an interim basis, to find some other work. I am not persuaded that that is necessarily the case, nor that such work would be significant enough such as to negate the consequences of not being reinstated on an interim basis. [57] A significant issue in the present case is that ADO resides in the farmhouse. On the one hand, the JFCT says it will be impacted by that continuing in that it will be unable to appoint a stock manager. On the other hand, ADO and his partner would be required to vacate the residence, at least until such time as a substantive determination is issued. On balance, I consider the arrangements relating to the accommodation favour ADO. [58] I conclude that the balance of convenience favours ADO. Where does the overall justice lie? [59] I have concluded that ADO has an arguable case and that the balance of convenience in this case favours ADO. I must now, standing back from the case, consider what the overall justice of the case requires I do.11 [60] ADO has been performing work at Chesterhope for a reasonably significant period of time and resides on the farm. He has performed farm work of some value for the duration of that time, and standing back from the case, I consider that the overall justice of the case requires that ADO be reinstated on an interim basis. [61] ADO’s application for interim reinstatement is successful. Order [62] The JFCT is to reinstate ADO to their employment in the role they were engaged in immediately prior to the dismissal. The JFCT is ordered to do so within seven days of the date of this determination. This is to allow time for any practical and administrative arrangements to be made in relation to compliance with this order. [63] The JFCT have leave to make application to the Authority should any practical issues arise relating to this order. Next steps [64] A further case management conference will be scheduled shortly for the purposes of setting a timetable for the Authority’s investigation. Costs [65] Costs are reserved pending consideration of ADO’s substantive claims. Rowan Anderson Member of the Employment Relations Authority 11 Klissers Farmhouse Bakeries Ltd v Harvest Bakeries Ltd [1985] 2 NZLR 129 (CA); X v Y Ltd and the New Zealand Stock Exchange [1992] 1 ERNZ 862 (EmpC), at 872.

case_name: RUIDONG XU v PIONEER EDUCATION AND IMMIGRATION SERVICES GROUP LIMITED
operative_excerpt: at one point that the true employer was Mr Zhu as he supervised Mr Xu. That said Mr Xu appears to have been clearly aware of the identity of the employer given he correctly cited it when lodging his claim. When I add comments and concessions he made I conclude any claim Mr Zhu might have personally employed Mr Xu has no basis. Finally, and given the parties agreement, the matter proceeded with Pioneer recognised as the correct respondent. Pioneer primarily provides education consultancy services to international students who predominately come from China. It also provides immigration consultancy services primarily aimed at those same students. The latter services are provided by employees licensed with the Immigration Advisers Authority though they are assisted by various support staff. Mr Xu says he was initially engaged as a student counsellor and was issued an essential skills work visa accordingly. He says he was subsequently compelled to engage in LIA work and this forms the basis of one of his grievances. That said he accepts that having had his role amended and LIA duties added, he did so as a provisionally registered LIA and was supervised in that role by Mr Zhu. By way of further background, Mr Xu adds Mr Zhu was found to have used non-compliant practices by the Immigration Advisers Complaints and Disciplinary Tribunal. Mr Xu also adds that three colleagues left between mid-July and mid-November 2019, meaning that he got a lot of extra work. This was largely LIA work and goes to the claim he was disadvantaged by having to perform that work. Mr Xu says that on 7 January 2020, and totally unheralded, he was simply told he was going to be dismissed. That was followed by an email headed “Personal issue about supervising capability and time engagement”. Included is the following: This is to confirm the following notices are listed for your reference: This is the official notice according to employment agreement clause 12, a three week notice to be given. The ending date is 28th of January 2020. The reason for termination of employment was explained today, majorly due to my limited time strength and capability, which cannot cater your needs of long-term career development. On 9 January, Mr Xu responded with an email questioning the decision. It closed by stating Mr Xu wished to remain at Pioneer and asking that Mr Zhu reconsider. That did not occur and while the parties met on 10 January the decision to dismiss was confirmed and there was a further email which reiterated Mr Zhu’s view he had the right to choose not to supervise Mr Xu any longer and give consideration to changing his life/work balance. The email goes on to suggest another LIA who had been mentioned in Mr Xu’s letter was in a better position as she could obtain a full, as opposed to provisional, licence before going on to say: I consider this as an opportunity for me to take a break, to simply well look after my engaged clients, rather than giving training and full monitoring provisional advisers daily practice for the last 8 years. I think I have the minimum right to make such a decision at this point. The email then discusses a further point before saying: “By considering your strong willingness to keep working at Pioneer, we can schedule a meeting to discuss variation of working scopes” and the possibility of finding a new LIA supervisor though the evidence confirms that if this occurred it would have been with an employer other than Pioneer. Suffice to say, nothing changed and Mr Xu’s last day of employment was 28 January 2020. Thereafter, he attempted to return to China in order to find work but his travel plans were stymied by the Covid pandemic. On 2 April, he raised a personal grievance challenging his dismissal and the change to his original role. The following day a further personal grievance was raised regarding the non-licensed immigration advisor practices. A third personal grievance followed concerning the bringing of religious practices into the workplace. A final and fourth personal grievance regarding the allegation Pioneer had not disclosed the true reasons for the dismissal was raised in July. Analysis Mr Xu’s first and prime claim is that he was unjustifiably dismissed. That it dismissed Mr Xu is conceded by Pioneer which means it is required to justify its decision. With respect to justification s 103A of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) states the issue: … must be determined, on an objective basis, [by considering] whether the employer’s actions, and how the employer acted were what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances at the time the dismissal … occurred. Traditionally and while issues of substance and process overlap and there is no such thing as a firm delineation, separation has often been used for analytical purposes especially as the requirements of s 103A of the Employment Relations Act (the Act) are enshrined in statute and a number have a procedural focus.1 As a bare minimum and having regard to its resources, an employer contemplating dismissal is required to conduct a sufficient enquiry prior to dismissing. A sufficient investigation requires, as a bare minimum, the employer put its concerns, allow an opportunity to respond and consider the response with an open mind. Mr Xu says none of that happened with his first knowledge of the dismissal being advice it was to occur. Mr Zhu essentially concedes that was correct and expresses the view he thought he had the right to bow to personal pressures and cease supervising Mr Xu which effectively meant he was no longer employable. The concession does however mean Pioneer had no chance of complying with the 1 Sections 103A(3)(b) to (d) of the Employment Relations Act 2000 requirements of s103A of the Act and that was recognised by its lawyers when they later wrote: While Mr Zhu was of the understanding that termination of your employment was justified at the time (namely, he did not have the capacity to supervise you any longer), he is realistic in his approach and understands it is futile to argue termination of your employment was justified in accordance with the test of justification in the Act. While termination of your employment was not intended to be malicious, Mr Zhu accepts that it was misguided.2 The simple fact is, as conceded, the dismissal was absent any process or consideration of Mr Xu’s situation and a lack of resource cannot excuse such all- encompassing deficiency.3 The dismissal is unjustified. Turning to the disadvantage claims which I shall consider in the order each was listed in the Statement of Problem. For a claim of unjustified disadvantage to succeed there must be an action of the employer which operated to the employee’s disadvantage in the workplace. As already said the first claim raised in the statement or problem, namely that Pioneer failed to advise the true reasons for Mr Xu’s dismissal, was withdrawn. The second claim was that Pioneer unilaterally altered Mr Xu’s role from Student Counsellor to Licensed Immigration Adviser (LIA). The claim is that Mr Xu was disadvantaged by virtue of having his immigration status put at risk by reason of a unilateral change in duties contrary to his visa which described him as a Student Counsellor. He also claims to have been overworked by reason of the departure of his colleagues with a resulting need to then concentrate on LIA duties and that he was “deskilled” by reason of doing less student advisory work. The evidence is clear – the LIA duties were not imposed. Mr Xu agreed, and this is reflected in his closing submission, that he enjoyed the “hybrid” nature of the role as it offered experience in both education and immigration consultancy.4 To that I add the fact I largely accept the evidence Mr Xu in fact preferred that work and here I note the Pioneer’s submission where it was said: 2 Letter to Mr Xu dated 13 October 2020 3 The Salad Bowl Ltd v Howe-Thornley [2013] NZEmpC 152 at [94] and [95] 4 Closing submission at [13] It is notable that he is also seeking compensation for a change in his duties to immigration advisory work and at the same time seeking compensation for a dismissal that could have been avoided had he accepted the offer in January 2020 to relinquish immigration advisory work and revert to education consultancy work.5 The evidence supports that submission. It also supports the submission Mr Xu’s job description, which Immigration New Zealand had when it approved Mr Xu’s visa, was sufficiently wide as it includes immigration work. Finally it has to be noted Mr Xu’s visa was not affected and the main disadvantage claimed never occurred. Similarly, and while he did raise issues about workload, the evidence is that Pioneer responded by both giving additional pay and three staff to assist. There is no evidence that other than constant grumbling to colleagues about workload, he found Pioneers response inadequate or that if he did he raised it with the company. For this type of disadvantage to succeed there must also be evidence the employer rejected an opportunity to address it and here the evidence is the opposite – it did address the issue when raised and were not told its response was inadequate. The third claim was that Mr Xu was required to follow non-compliant LIA procedures. Other than the reference to issues with the licensing Authority there is little evidence. Such breaches, if they occurred, are in the domain of another jurisdiction and while he complains he was at risk of proceedings in the relevant Authority no such event occurred and no such disadvantage materialised. In any event as a supervised LIA the bulk of any risk would fall upon the supervisor. Aside from the fact supporting evidence is sparse, I conclude the claim appears to have been brought to support the overwork claim. On that I have already commented. Given the points above this claim also fails. The final claim is that Mr Xu was disadvantaged by having his employer’s religion practiced in the workplace absent consultation. Mr Xu says as he did not participate he was disadvantaged as he felt excluded from his colleagues who did attend.6 5 Closing submission at [37](b)(i) 6 Closing submission at [50] This claim must also fail as aside from the fact there is no evidence of exclusion, I note. Mr Zhu’s religious views and practices were well promulgated and Mr Xu knew of them, or should have, when he was employed. To that I add his evidence that while he did not attend there was no compulsion he do so and no penalty for not. While he says this did not alleviate feeling of peer pressure and a feeling of exclusion there is again no evidence he raised the issue. Indeed he accepts he didn’t as by the time he considered this an issue he was already leaving. The implication of that evidence is until the dismissal there was no disadvantage which severely undermines the claim. It too shall fail. For the reasons above I conclude Mr Xu was unjustifiably dismissed but that his disadvantage claims fail. That conclusion means the question of remedies must be considered. For the dismissal Mr Xu seeks lost wages and compensation pursuant to s123(1)(c)(i) of the Act. Section 128(2) of the Act requires the payment of three months wages or the actual loss if less though I this instance Mr Xu asks I exercise my discretion and increase that amount without saying to what. That is not a discretion I intend exercising as the evidence is Mr Xu made no attempt to mitigate his loss in New Zealand, instead choosing to return to China. That he was then stymied in his attempt to do so by reason of the covid pandemic was not the fault of Pioneer and should not be visited upon them. Indeed the evidence would suggest the reason for the return to China was most likely the ending of a long standing personal relationship and while Mr Xu now blames that on his dismissal there is no evidence to support that proposition. The award shall be the three months payable under that Act. There are also a range of claims for the reimbursement of monies lost as a result of the dismissal but the bulk of these appear related to Mr Xu’s decision to return to China. As already said, that was his choice with the evidence suggesting other issues influencing his decision. Others relate to medical costs and psychiatrists fees but the relevant dates correspond with the relationship breakup and not the dismissal. To that I add Mr Xu’s evidence he was also stressed as a result of covid and once again I reiterate Pioneer cannot be held responsible for that and its effects. No award shall therefore be made. With respect to compensation, and while specific amounts were claimed for the alleged disadvantages, Mr Xu does not specify an amount for the dismissal though he does refer to a generous offer of settlement Mr Zu made in an open letter. While I accept hurt must emanate from the dismissal there was little direct evidence of the effect it had on him with the evidence offered being a diverse mix of alleged effects from that, the disadvantages, the loss of Mr Xu’s personal relationship and the effect of covid. Given my conclusion there is only one of those I can compensate and again I reiterate there was little direct evidence and definitely none that would come close to warranting an award of the magnitude of the offer Mr Xu rejected. Having considered the evidence and current levels of compensation I consider $15,000 appropriate. Finally the conclusion Mr Xu has a grievance and remedies accrue means I must also consider whether or not those remedies should be reduced by reasons of contributory conduct.7 The short answer is no as there is no evidence he contributed to the failures which ensured he succeeded with his dismissal grievance. Conclusion and Orders For the above reasons I conclude Mr Xu has a personal grievance in that he was unjustifiably dismissed. As a result I order Pioneer Education and Immigration Services Group Limited pay Ruidong Xu: (a) Three months wages being those lost as a result of the dismissal; and (b) A further $15,000.00 (fifteen thousand dollars) as compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings pursuant to section 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act; While Mr Xu has been successful he was self-represented which means recoverable cost are limited to the Authority’s filing fee. Having said that I note the 7 Section 124 of the Employment Relations Act 2000 magnitude of the open offer means it is quite possible there is a Calderbank in existence, though the Courts conclusions in Fifita v Dunedin Casinos8 would suggest its benefit might well be limited to ensuring costs lie where they fall. It is my preliminary view that is what should occur here. If either party disagrees they should serve a memorandum on costs within 14 days of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum the other party will have 14 days to lodge any reply. Michael Loftus Member of the Employment Relations Authority 8 Fifita v Dunedin Casinos Ltd [2013] NZEpmC 171

case_name: JOLINE GUNTER v KIDS WORLD CHILDCARE LOWER HUTT LIMITED T/A ALL ABOUT CHILDREN
operative_excerpt: IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY WELLINGTON I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI TE WHANGANUI Ā TARA ROHE [2024] NZERA 98 3139505 BETWEEN JOLINE GUNTER Applicant AND KIDS WORLD CHILDCARE LOWER HUTT LIMITED T/A ALL ABOUT CHILDREN Respondent Member of Authority: Sarah Kennedy-Martin Representatives: Dave Cain, advocate for the Applicant Mike Harrison, advocate for the Respondent Submissions and 4 December 2023 and 5 February 2024 from Applicant affidavits received: 6 December 2023 and 12 February 2024 from Respondent Determination: 22 February 2024 COSTS DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY In its substantive determination of 20 November 2023, the Authority found that Jolene Gunter’s dismissal was unjustified and she was awarded compensation of $18,000.00 for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings and $13,000.00 for lost wages as a result of the dismissal.1 The Authority reserved costs and encouraged the parties to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. They have been unable to do that and both parties have now provided submissions and affidavits on costs. 1 Joline Gunter v Kids World Childcare Lower Hutt Limited [2023] NZERA 686. The parties have different positions and recollections about offers made on the day of the investigation meeting and what type of offer/s were made. Kids World Child Care Limited (Kids World), the respondent, submits an offer on the day of the investigation meeting supersedes a Calderbank offer made by Ms Gunter, the applicant, five days before the meeting. I have not found it necessary to resolve the conflict in their positions on this aspect of the matter because any offers made in the course of discussions to resolve the matter between them on the day of the investigation meeting are not considered to be valid Calderbank offers because the stage the proceeding was at. Ms Gunter’s submissions Ms Gunter seeks an award of costs for a one-day hearing in the sum of $8,321.56. This is based on preparation time for one day of meeting time plus submissions on costs with a 50 percent uplift to the daily tariff because of an effective Calderbank offer, plus the filing fee of $71.56. Ms Gunter made a Calderbank offer on 15 November 2022 for $21,000.00, inclusive of costs. This was rejected by Kids World. The total award for remedies in the Authority came to $31,000.00. Kids World Child Care submissions Kids World submits the daily tariff for a one-day meeting would be appropriate. It rejects the uplift sought by Ms Gunter saying the earlier Calderbank offer was invalidated by further offers made and rejected on the day of the meeting. As set out above, I do not intend to take settlement offers made on the day into account because it was too late for valid Calderbank offers to be made. Costs Costs are a matter of discretion. The discretion is to be exercised in accordance with principle and not arbitrarily. The main principle in the exercise of the discretion is that costs follow the event. If a party is successful, they will be entitled to an award of costs. Ms Gunter was successful. The Authority’s investigation meeting time amounted to just short of one full day. The starting point for costs based on the Authority’s daily tariff is $4,500.00 for the first day. The Authority can from that starting point consider whether there are factors justifying an increase or decrease in costs. This can include whether an effective Calderbank offer was unreasonably refused.2 Calderbank offer The consequences of unreasonably rejecting an effective Calderbank offer is that costs awarded may be increased. The Calderbank offer attached to Ms Gunter’s submissions was marked “without prejudice except as to costs” and it informed Kids World in writing it was a Calderbank offer and should Ms Gunter be successful she reserved the right to bring a copy of the offer to the Authority’s attention and seek an uplift to any costs award. There is a difference of $10,000.00 between the Calderbank offer of $21,000.00 made by Ms Gunter and the Authority’s award of $31,000.00. Given the Calderbank offer was made five days before the investigation meeting it is likely preparation for the meeting had been completed prior to that day. However, it was still in advance of the investigation meeting so costs from the day could have been saved had the offer been accepted. I consider that had Kids World accepted that offer, it would have been in a better position and a modest uplift to reflect the timing of that offer of $750.00 would be appropriate. Orders Kids World Childcare Lower Hutt Limited is ordered to pay Joline Gunter $5,250.00 in costs and $71.56 for the filing fee. Sarah Kennedy-Martin Member of the Employment Relations Authority 2 Practice Direction of the Employment Relations Authority Te Ratonga Ahumana Taimahi

case_name: YIPING CHEN v ARMSTRONG PRESTIGE LIMITED
operative_excerpt: Yiping claimed had been speaking this information and when’. In her oral evidence I found Ms Wilkins straight forward. She accepted that she did not reply to the ‘commission’ issues as a grievance but rather sent the information requested including details of ‘all the cars Yiping had sold with APL and payments received.’ Emails at the time support this. 7 [21] Ms Chen says that APL consented to the grievance4 by which I take it she suggests that in responding to the 8 January 2020 letter APL engaged with the grievance details beyond that date and could not later be able to reasonably argue that it had not. I do not find these responses support this may constitute consent to raise the grievances outside of time beyond responding to the specified details reading the commission payments. The only thing specified as a reason for the ‘dismissal’ (which I read as a reason for Ms Chen to have resigned in relation to her unjustified constructive dismissal claim) was that she ‘was incorrectly and consistently paid commission on sales, and was not provided with accurate information related to sales in a manner which fundamentally breached the terms of her employment agreement’. To that extent I find there was at the very least sufficient detail to reply to. [22] Further details were promised in the 8 January 2020 letter for AP to respond to about the constructive dismissal grievance. Any further details were not provided by Ms Chen until 22 January 2022 when she lodged her grievance in the Authority. By that time, her reasons for saying she was constructively dismissed, or by then also disadvantaged in her employment, had expanded beyond just the stated issue about her commission payments as a reason for the dismissal to include issues she had with her manager and or AP relating to her working long hours with no breaks, being required to work when she had childcare issues, having a suggestion made to her to resign in relation to specific circumstances connected to a survey she completed and being discriminated against in relation to family status, ethnicity and gender. While these things may potentially fit within details to explain a constructive dismissal claim or unjustified actions I accept the submission for APL that there was none of this detail provided to AP to respond to any of these things until Ms Chen lodged her claim in the Authority. [23] Even if I accept Ms Chen did not receive the survey information that she requested through her representative on 5 December 2029 from APL, there was no detail given to APL in the 5 December 2019 about the reason for this information. Even if I then consider the reference in the 8 January 2020 letter to wanting the survey information urgently because ‘it 4 Applicant’s Closing Submissions dated 14 November 2023, paragraph 6 referencing emails exchanged regarding the commission payments and provision of information. 8 may be material to the claim of constructive dismissal’ this was never followed up by Ms Chen with any further details until Ms Chen lodged her claim in the Authority. [24] I further note that Ms Chen claims that the Authority gave her permission to raise further disadvantage claims in her Amended Statement of Problem. However, I agree with the submission from AP that she is mistaken about this ‘permission’. She was asked to clarify her original claims. [25] Accordingly, considering the above I find that Ms Chen raised a personal grievance within the 90-day timeframe for unjustified constructive dismissal but only in relation to saying that this was based on her not receiving commission payments throughout her employment and not receiving information about them. I find she has not raised any other grievances within time and will now consider whether there are exceptional circumstances for her to do so and then whether it would be just to grant this leave. [26] I note that AP submits that if I were to reach the above conclusion that Ms Chen has raised a constructive dismissal grievance linked to her commission payments (which I have) I should consider s103(3) of the Act. That section says that an ‘unjustified action’ relating to a disadvantage personal grievance that derives solely from a contractual dispute cannot be treated as a grievance but as a dispute. [27] I am not persuaded that I should consider this issue at this preliminary stage. It is obviously for Ms Chen to provide her evidence to support her grievance. I note for now that Ms Chen’s grievance was raised under the head of unjustified dismissal and not as disadvantage in employment which is what s103(3) of the Act relates to. If Ms Chen did not raise her grievance(s) within time are there ‘exceptional circumstances’ that caused the delay and if so is it just to grant leave for Ms Chen to raise her grievance(s) out of time? [28] The Supreme Court5 has affirmed6 a definition of ‘exceptional circumstances’ under s 115 of the Act as ‘unusual, outside of the common run, perhaps something more than special 5 Creedy v Commissioner of Police [2008]NZSC 31 at [31] 6 Quoting Wilkins & Field Ltd v Fortune [1998] ERNZ (CA) at [76]. 9 and less than extraordinary.’ It found this definition accorded with ordinary English usage. However, it also noted that the ‘short time limit of 90 days, and the potential serious consequences for employees if not being able to bring a personal grievance, support an interpretation [of ‘exceptional circumstances’ under s 115] which does not limit unduly the power to extend time. The prohibition in s 113 on challenging a dismissal otherwise than by a personal grievance reinforces this point.’7 [29] However, the Court in the above matter also said at [33]: we also emphasise that Parliament has imposed a 90-day limit to ensure that employers are notified promptly of alleged grievances. Time should therefore be extended only if exceptional circumstances are truly established and, in addition, the overall justice of the case (which includes taking account of the position of an employer facing a later claim) so requires. [my italicised emphasis added]. [30] Ms Chen says there were ‘exceptional circumstances’ under two subsections of s 115 being: (a) where the employee has been so affected or traumatised by the matter giving rise to the grievance that he or she was unable to properly consider raising the grievance within the period specified in section 114(1) [90-day period to raise a grievance]; and (b) where the employee made reasonable arrangements to have the grievance raised on his or her behalf by an agent of the employee, and the agent unreasonably failed to ensure that the grievance was raised within the required time. [31] If I am satisfied that the delay in raising her grievance was caused by one or both of these ‘exceptional circumstances’ I must then consider if it is just to grant leave for Ms Chen to bring her grievance out of time. If I do, I must then direct the parties to mediation ‘to seek to mutually resolve the grievances’ allowed then to be brought.8 7 Creedy v Commissioner of Police [2008] NZSC 31 at [32] 8 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 114(3) to (6). 10 Was Ms Chen so affected or traumatised by the matter giving rise to the grievance that she was unable to properly consider raising the grievance within 90 days? [32] AP submits that I do not have sufficient evidence on which to make a finding that Ms Chen was traumatised and could not bring her grievance within time. I agree. I accept AP’s submission that there is guidance from the Employment Court that there is a ‘high standard of proof’ to meet this test and it would require ‘very substantial injury’ suffered by the employee for the entire 90-day period.9 Ms Chen refers to her friend having passed away and the representative she used leaving the firm. Both events I take to have been in the second part of 2020. The last communications from Ms Chen’s representative to AP about calculation of commissions owed were in August 2020. These things occurred after the 90th day for her to have raised her personal grievances that I have found are out of time. They could not then be linked to her being so traumatised by the matter giving rise to the grievance that she was unable because of the impact to raise her grievance within the 90-day period. [33] I do not find ‘exceptional circumstances’ under this part of Ms Chen’s application. Did Ms Chen make reasonable arrangements to have the grievances raised on her behalf by an agent and then did the agent unreasonably fail to ensure that the grievance was raised within time? [34] It is submitted for AP that Ms Chen did not make any reasonable arrangements to raise her grievances in a way that specified what they were so that AP could respond to them on 8 January 2020. For me to make that sort of finding I would need to hear from the agent involved or have some evidence beyond what I have before me. As noted above Ms Chen has not involved the representative in these proceedings. Ms Chen unexpectedly provided new evidence of emails between herself and the representative after the investigation meeting. AP’s reply was to say that I should not consider this evidence. I have considered this evidence which amounts to three brief emails between Ms Chen and the representative in December 2019 around the time she first met with that person. My findings below will show that my consideration of this evidence here does not work unfairly against AP’s right to be heard. 9 Telecom New Zealand Ltd v Morgan [2004] 2 ERNZ 9. 11 [35] The first email dated 4 December 2019 from Ms Chen to the representative shows Ms Chen had previously met the representative the day before for the first time. She refers to having sent the representative emails but not what they were or what they related to. She explains that she thinks she filled out two ’employee satisfaction’ surveys, one before and one after she says it was ‘suggested’ to her that she resign. [36] The second email from the representative to Ms Chen is dated 5 December and attaches for Ms Chen the 5 December 2019 letter sent to AP. The cover email is only two lines and includes ‘we will see what reply I get’ [from the 5 December 2019 letter] followed by a question asking, ‘When he suggested you resign, what exactly did he say?’. [37] The third email dated 6 December 2019 is from Ms Chen to the representative and appears to include Ms Chen’s reply to the above email in six sentences stating things she says were said to her by her manager in August 2019 that seem to reflect some of the allegations that Ms Chen has put before the Authority now but were not raised for response by AP in relation to her grievance claims within 90-days. [38] I find the content of these emails lack sufficient detail for me to form the view that Ms Chen wants me to take from them which is that she took reasonable steps to ensure her grievance was raised through her representative and her representative failed to do this. This is because I have no information about what Ms Chen’s instructions were that led to her sometime later instruct the representative to send the content of the 8 January 2020. [39] I further note that I have nothing to satisfy me that Ms Chen did anything to ensure she took reasonable steps to follow up on the ‘further details’ that were referred to in the 8 January 2020 letter that may then have enabled AP to respond or make sense of the claims about Ms Chen saying that the employer set out on a ‘course of action’ that induced her to resign; or that her employer provided misleading information to others about the reason she left her employment. That detail has taken a long time for Ms Chen to bring forward. After 8 January 2020 the only communications that Ms Chen instructed her representative to make focused solely on Ms Chen wanting further details about how her commission was calculated and putting forward what she considered it should be. The representative ceased 12 communicating about this from August 2020 and Ms Chen did nothing further to communicate with AP after this (until she lodged her claim in the Authority). [40] I have paused to consider whether Ms Chen was unlikely to have had the ability to understand the timeframe to raise her grievance with more detail than the 8 January 2020 letter. I accept the submission for AP that Ms Chen is not without ability. She has submitted formal written applications and written submissions with case references. She has explained to me she her studies involve learning about the law. [41] Standing back from the above I am not satisfied Ms Chen has shown I should find that an exceptional circumstance exists whereby she took reasonable steps to raise her grievances in time and that her agent did not do this. That is a serious finding to make in the absence of sufficient evidence and the participation of the agent. Even if I had found exceptional circumstances under this heading, I would have had to still then consider whether it would be just to allow Ms Chen to bring the grievances. I accept the submission from AP that this would be difficult to defend as they relate to conversations had and the meanings taken from them over three years ago. I would also have likely concluded as part of considering whether it would be just to allow leave to be granted that Ms Chen is not without the opportunity to seek remedies by continuing to have her claims heard within the category of breaches of her IEA and or statute. Much of that material crosses over with the things she says support the grievance claims that I find have been raised too late. In that sense I would have considered it may not have been just to allow leave especially given the length of time passed without any further details provided for AP to respond to. Summary of findings [42] I find Ms Chen raised her personal grievance for unjustified dismissal by constructive dismissal against AP within the statutory 90-day timeframe but only in relation to her allegation that a reason for the ‘dismissal’ was that Ms Chen was ‘incorrectly and consistently paid commission on sales and was not provided with accurate information related to sales in a manner which fundamentally breached the terms of her employment agreement.’ 13 [43] I do not find Ms Chen raised any other personal grievances within the 90-day time frame as contained in her Amended Statement of Problem dated 31 July 2023. [44] I find there are no ‘exceptional circumstances’ to support granting leave for Ms Chen to bring the grievances referred to in [43] above outside of the 90-day time frame to do so. Costs [45] Costs are reserved and will be dealt with as part of the substantive investigation process. Next steps [46] The Authority will continue as scheduled to hear Ms Chen’s other claims as they relate to either statutory or contractual entitlements or breaches as set out in her Amended Statement of Problem dated 31 July 2023 and in relation to her unjustified constructive dismissal claim as it is referred to above at [42]. [47] The Authority will arrange a brief phone conference call as soon as possible to schedule the provision of any further evidence for the scheduled investigation meeting which is currently set down to occur in April 2024. Antoinette Baker Member of the Employment Relations Authority

case_name: YFX v CHIEF OF THE NEW ZEALAND DEFENCE FORCE
operative_excerpt: 27 May, Defence advised it would not enter into a record of settlement at the upcoming mediation. That is said to be a clear breach of the duty of good faith. On 23 June, YFX advised she was considering resignation, primarily on the grounds she could no longer suffer long term leave without pay with eight months having passed since November 2019, the lack of good faith on NZDF’s part given its obvious reluctance to try and resolve the employment relationship problem and a resulting loss of trust and confidence in management. YFX says she considered NZDF’s reply was both senseless and insensitive. That led to her confirming her resignation on 6 July, YFX confirmed the resignation. It was accepted and her last day was 5 August 2020. Analysis As already noted YFX claims that she had been disadvantaged by multiple acts of NZDF which when considered as a totality led her to conclude the relationship was no longer tenable and her resulting resignation constituted a constructive dismissal. In submission YFX states: Based on the large volumes of information provided by both parties, the new information sufficed at the Authority’s investigation meeting and the cross examination of 12 witnesses, it is clear that the downward turning point of the working relationship between YFX and Ms Pointon landed on two events that were concurrently evolving - the NZSIS security clearance and YFX’s complaint against Ms Edney’s coughing. I agree and note that downward track ended with YFX’s resignation. It is that along with other factors that leads me, notwithstanding the list of pleaded disadvantages, to treat this as a constructive dismissal claim as was also claimed. The other factors are as follows. First a number of the purported disadvantages were not raised as formal personal grievances within 90 days of their alleged occurrence and there is no application they be 13 allowed out of time pursuant to s 114(3) of the Act. While YFX correctly argues she aired her concerns that falls short of the requirement the employer be given clear notice those concerns constitute a grievance and that was not advised until 11 December 2019. By then more than 90 days had passed since a number of the events pleaded as disadvantages including the security clearance (October 2018 to March 2019), the letter of expectation (12 July 2019), the failure to address the noise complaint which had been raised early in the year and the failure to justify the salary review. The same concern applies to the removal of duties which occurred prior to May, the failure to set adequate performance objectives which was an issue early in the year, and the resetting of YFX’s salary rating (though it is arguable that can constitute a grievance). Second there is a disconnect between the pleadings and the way the disadvantages were listed and argued in submission. Third, and while it was stated in submission that YFX’s compensatory award should recognise the disadvantages, remedies were sought and argued as a single totality. Fourth and as a result of the way the evidence was presented and the case argued NZDF also adopted this approach. In Auckland etc. Shop Employees etc IUOW v Woolworths (NZ) Ltd3 the Court of Appeal held constructive dismissal includes, but is not limited to, cases where: (a) An employer gives an employee a choice between resigning or being dismissed; (b) An employer has followed a course of conduct with the deliberate and dominant purpose of coercing an employee to resign. (c) A breach of duty by the employer causes an employee to resign. In Wellington etc Clerical Workers etc IUOW v Greenwich4 the Court stated that for a dismissal to be constructive: It is not enough that the employer’s conduct is inconsiderate and causes some unhappiness to the employee. It must be dismissive or repudiatory conduct. 3 (1985) ERNZ Sel Cas 136; 2 NZLR 372 (CA) 4 (1983) ERNZ Sel Cas 95; [1983] ACJ 965 14 While a simplistic summary of more complex law, the underlying assumption is actions or words of the employer amounted to a breach which induced a subsequently proffered resignation. It is for the applicant to convince me that is the case. There must also be a causal link between the employer’s conduct and the tendering of the resignation5 and the possibility of resignation should be foreseeable.6 When asked why she resigned YFX commented that aside from a view she was being treated very unfairly by virtue of the various events pleaded as disadvantages, the final straw was NZDF’s unwillingness the address her concerns. Having considered the evidence and submissions I conclude YFX was constructively dismissed by virtue of a breach of duty by NZDF with that breach being its failure to properly address the issues YFX’s raised. While I have decided against treating the alleged disadvantages as standalone claims, I do conclude that YFX was, if not improperly treated in every way she claims, given more than adequate reasons to have concerns and raise them. In this regard I also note there was a contractual obligation to address concerns, even if informal, quickly. While NZDF argue that when YFX complained the change was reversed, consultation occurred and it was then reintroduced the damage had been done and the outcome took the appearance of having been predetermined. For example, and while the security clearance was conducted by NZSIS which is a separate organisation for whose actions NZDF cannot be held responsible, it is clear concerns about the process were held with NZDF’s Chief Mental Health Officer, who became involved in this process, classifying the clearance process as unduly prolonged and invasive with questions being asked that appeared, at least to YFX, to be irrelevant. I also have concerns about the removal of duties which NZDF witnesses described as occurring while YFX was on leave with the newly arranged processes simply being allowed to continue after her return. This was despite a contractual provision which while allowing jobs to evolve and permitting NZDF to change them, required prior consultation. That didn’t occur before the change was first implemented. 5 Z v A [1993] 2 ERNZ 469 6 Weston v Advkit Para Legal Services Ltd [2010] NZEmpC 140 15 There was then the noise complaint. Accepting the evidence concerning noise levels was informally gathered it did show there was an issue. Once appraised of that issue NZDF, as a PCBU under the Health and Safety at Work Act, was required to address it. Put simply, it failed to do so and then aggravated the situation by advising YFX that she faced potential disciplinary action essentially for having raised it. This situation was not assisted by NZDF advancing Ms Edney’s grievance that she was being bullied by what was, on the face of it, a legitimate concern. Indeed, Ms Pointon accepted the complaint was valid but contended the persistence with which it as being aired was what was upsetting Ms Edney. I might suggest that if it had been addressed persistence might not have been required. Further issues then arose with NZDF combining and confusing processes. While I accept the conditional security clearance required addressing it was improper to also introduce issues of performance and alleged staff concerns in the same meeting. It was also improper to then, as frequently happened, combine requests for medical information purportedly to assist YFX with treats of disciplinary action and performance concerns. This is especially so when it is considered NZDF already had the information it sought as was evidenced by a change in the office layout designed to address YFX’s issues. NZDF was also being warned its approach was damaging YFX and invoking a number of her mental health triggers which meant to continue with its approach aw s fraught. The pursuit of the alleged performance concerns is also concerning in light of the admission by a couple of NZDF’s witnesses that YFX’s role was poorly defined. It should have been properly defined before she was judged against purported failures to achieve as required, especially as she no longer knew what was required and was advising accordingly. There is another crucial fact and that is that both parties agree the culture within the team was ‘toxic’ with NZDF accepting there were factions with one trying to undermine YFX. In such circumstances I am left wondering why she was the only person being held up as potentially incompatible with her colleagues. Finally I note the failure to produce the support plan that the evidence now establishes was written in November 2019 and therefore available. Indeed there were two versions but 16 more importantly it makes one wonder why NZDF was adamant it needed YFX’s health information when it clearly had enough to develop the required plan. As already said it follows YFX had grounds for concern and these she formally raised on 11 December. Not only that she also advised “that if there is no expeditious resolution to this matter, it would be impossible for YFX to continue working n current conditions. It will leave YFX with no option but to resign” which clearly fulfils the foreseeability requirement. It also follows it should have come as no great surprise YFX health deteriorated and she succumbed to the pressure, especially as the evidence shows NZDF was aware of her medical situation and she had reached out to a number of people within defence for assistance. It is here I consider NZDF acted in breach to an extent it ensured resignation would occur. It first delayed its response. It then, despite my order to mediation, aggravated the situation by avoiding dates and then advising it would not settle. In such circumstances, and given her advice the situation had to be addressed or she would have no option but to resign, it must have come as no surprise when she did. The failure to address YFX’s concerns in a timely and proper fashion is a breach and renders this a constructive dismissal. The conclusion YFX has a personal grievance having been constructively dismissed raises the question of remedies. She seeks compensation and the reimbursement of wages lost while she remained in the workplace but without pay on the grounds this was the result of NZDF’s failure to address her concerns. There is no claim for wages after the resignation was tendered, probably because YFX, now considering herself free to do so, went and almost immediately obtained a new job. The wage claim is for $31,488.78 being the difference between what YFX would have earnt minus various sums she was paid which primarily appear to be for public holidays along with a special pay of 10 days in February. The problem I have with this claim is that she had exhausted her sick leave so on the face of it there is no entitlement. That said the argument is NZDF should be liable given its repeated failure to address legitimate issues, was the cause of the illness and the leave. That 17 unfortunately is not what the medical certification says – it says she was suffering stress that she attributes to the work environment. It doesn’t go so far as to say that was the case. Add to that the fact a large number of the disadvantageous acts were raised out of time I am left with an inadequate causative link. There shall be no award of lost wages. Turning now to compensation. The amount sought is significant with a suggestion I consider a minimum of $50,000. The supporting evidence, both medical and that of YFX and her support witnesses, was extremely strong. There is talk of self-harm, and feeling of discrimination as a result of her health issues when previously she had been held up by NZDF as an example of what people in her situation could achieve, self-doubt, withdrawal from relationships with colleagues and friends. Indeed there was a list of some 23 effects I the written brief of evidence. YFX also spoke to the effects of these events during the investigation and it was, in my view, patently obvious from that evidence that she had suffered significant psychological harm. While I feel constrained in respect to awarding wages, and while I have also refrained from finding separate disadvantage personal grievances (largely because they were not properly raised in time) there is no doubt a number of NZDF’s actions, and its failure to address key and legitimate concerns before ignoring warning signs it was advised of and in any event should have been aware of, contributed to both the harm YFX felt and the eventual outcome. Add to that the fact the final straw which ultimately caused the resignation was wholly of NZDF’s making and that it had been put on notice that to act as it ultimately did would lead to a resignation I conclude and significant compensatory sum is warranted reflecting the adverse effects on YFX. Having considered the evidence and recent precedent I consider the sum of $40,000 appropriate. The conclusion YFX has a grievance and remedies accrue means I must also consider whether or not those remedies should be reduced by reasons of contributory conduct.7 It simply 7 Section 124 of the Employment Relations Act 2000 18 cannot be suggested she contributed to the events which finally brought about the resignation - namely the avoidance of addressing her legitimate concerns so the answer is no. YFX has asked that her identity and detail is her medical condition not be published. It is very difficult not to mention the medical situation in a situation such as this though I do accept it is sensitive and the details should not be publicly linked to YFX. That can be achieved by ordering the non-publication of anything which might identify her and therefore link her to the conditions described. Conclusion and Orders For the above reasons I conclude YFX has a personal grievance in that she has been constructively dismissed. As a result, I order the New Zealand Defence Force pay YFX the sum of $40,000 (forty thousand dollars) as compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings pursuant to s 123(1)()(i) of the Act. I also order a prohibition on the publication of anything that might identify the applicant in this matter.8 Costs are reserved with the parties encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. If they are not able to do so and an Authority determination on costs is needed YFX may, as the successful party, lodge and then should serve a memorandum on costs within 14 days of the date of issue of the written determination in this matter. From the date of service of that memorandum VNPL will have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. The parties could expect the Authority to determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual notional daily rate unless particular circumstances or factors required an upward or downward adjustment of that tariff.9 Michael Loftus Member of the Employment Relations Authority 8 Clause 10 of schedule 2 of the Employment Relations Act 2000 9 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs, see www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1.
